NOTICE OF PUBLIC HEARING AND AGENDA
NAVAJO COUNTY BOARD OF SUPERVISORS
Tuesday, December 10, 2019
ONE OR MORE SUPERVISORS MAY ATTEND VIA VIDEO AND/OR TELEPHONICALLY 
The Navajo County Board of Supervisors will hold a meeting open to the public on Tuesday, December 10, 2019, in the Supervisors’
Chamber in the Navajo County Governmental Complex, Holbrook, Arizona. The Board may vote to meet in a closed executive
session to discuss certain matters as indicated on the following agenda. The Board may meet in executive session pursuant to
A.R.S. § 38-431.03(A) (3) for legal advice on any item.
Persons with disabilities who need accommodation to attend or participate in the meeting may contact the Clerk of the Board’s office
at (928) 524-4053; at least 48 hours prior to the meeting so an accommodation can be arranged.
Items on the agenda may be considered out of order at the Chairman’s discretion. A copy of the agenda background material
provided to the Board, with the exception of items to be considered in executive session, is available for public inspection at Navajo
County website, www.navajocountyaz.gov 
9:00 a.m. Call To Order:  Invocation and Pledge of Allegiance
           
1. CALL TO THE PUBLIC: Individuals may address the Board on any relevant issue for up to 5
minutes. At the close of the call to the public, Board members may not respond to any comments
but may respond to criticism, ask staff to review a matter or ask that a matter be placed on a
future agenda.
 
 
2. CONSENT AGENDA: These items are considered to be routine or administrative in nature and
will be approved in a single motion. A Board member may request for any item to be removed
from the consent agenda and considered on the regular agenda:
 
 
a. Minutes: November 12, 2019 Regular Meeting and November 15, 2019 Special Meeting  
 
b. Warrant & Voucher Report over $1000 November 2019  
 
c. Constable Reports: Holbrook Precinct #1, October and November; Winslow Precinct #2,
September and October; Snowflake Precinct #3, October and November; Kayenta Precinct #4,
October; Show Low Precinct #5, November and Pinetop-Lakeside Precinct #6, September and
November 2019
 
 
d. Clerk of Superior Court Report October 2019  
 
e. Juvenile Probation Report October 2019  
 
f. Justice Court Reports: Holbrook Precinct #1, Winslow Precinct #2, Snowflake Precinct #3,
Kayenta Precinct #4, Show Low Precinct #5, Pinetop-Lakeside Precinct #6 October 2019
 
 
g. Name an existing unnamed road in the Heber area as "Spotted Saddle Trail" in Section 30,
Township 12 North, Range 17 East 
 
 
h. Annual letter to the Board of Supervisors stating that there are no changes to the boundary lines
for the school districts in Navajo County

<!-- page 2 -->
i. Approval of 50 Back Tax Land Parcels sold over the counter in the amount of $24,461.00  
 
j. Acceptance of Back Tax Land List and authorization to publish the notice of the same
scheduling the 2019 Back Tax Land On-Line Auction to begin on February 10, 2019, at 9:00
a.m.
 
 
k. Intergovernmental Agreement between the Sheriff's Office and cities of Winslow and Show
Low and Towns of Snowflake and Taylor regarding FY20 Byrne grant funding
 
 
l. ARRF Request for Holbrook Junior High School Anti-Bullying Campaign reimbursement not to
exceed $250.00
 
 
m. Legal representation of Navajo County by the Arizona Attorney General's Office in appeals for
tax year 2020 in Centurylink Corp. v. ADOR & Navajo County et. al.,  TX-2019-001726, and
Transwestern v. ADOR & Navajo County et. al., TX-2019-001725
 
 
n. Agreement with Gateway Oasis IV LLC for transitioning and acquiring a public easement from
the Arizona State Land Department
 
 
o. Certify FY17 AMENDED Fill the Gap Allocation  
 
p. Certify FY18 Fill the Gap Revenue  
 
q. Fill the Gap Certification Statement for FY19  
 
r. Donation to the White Mountain Apache Game Rangers, a 2005 Chevrolet 2500 4x4 Pick-Up
that has served its useful purpose and has no value
 
 
s. Designate Supervisor Jason Whiting as Navajo County's LPC representative for 2020  
 
t. Letter to the Arizona Department of Environmental Quality Proposed Program Roadmap for the
assumption of the Clean Water Act § 404 permitting process
 
 
u. Acknowledge receipt of the complete real property Assessment Roll of Navajo County for the
Tax Year 2020 and direct the Clerk to accept it for filing, pursuant to A.R.S.§ 42-15153
 
 
v. Resolution Number 30-19, formalizing the Extinguishment of a 20' and a 26' Public Easement
for parcels 212-29-001, 002, 003A & 003B as previously approved on August 13, 2019
 
 
w. Fiscal Year 19/20 Fund Transfers  
 
x. Memorandum of Understanding between the Navajo County Sheriff's Office and the United
States Marshals Service for the Violent Offender Task Force

<!-- page 3 -->
3. EMPLOYEE RECOGNITION:  
 
a. Navajo County Recognizes the following employees for their excellence in personal performance
far exceeding organization expectations: Vicci Ramsay-Chapman (Sheriff); Donna Hurstrom
(Board of Supervisors), Joel Johnston (Facilities Management); and Ronald Smith (Court
Administration).
 
Presented By: Lea Petersen
 
4. BOARD OF SUPERVISORS:  
 
a. Presentation to Blue Ridge High School Boys' Soccer Team for winning the State Championship.  
Presented By: Chairwoman Dawnafe Whitesinger
 
b. Presentation to Navajo County 4H Horse Club for their representation of Navajo County at the
State Horse Show.
 
Presented By: Mike Sample
 
c. PUBLIC HEARING: Consideration of a Liquor License Owner Transfer for Luis Fernando
Vargas Ventura at Grumpy Jakes located at 3973 W. White Mountain Boulevard, Lakeside,
Arizona.
 
Presented By: Donna Hurstrom
 
5. SHERIFF'S OFFICE:  
 
a. Presentation on service retirement of K-9 Legend.  
Presented By: Chief Deputy Sheriff Randy Moffitt
 
b. PUBLIC HEARING: Consideration and possible adoption of Resolution Number 31-19,
approving the collection of administrative fees for vehicles towed/seized during the investigation
of ARS Title 13, Chapter 34 Drug Offense violations.
 
Presented By: Deputy Chief Don Griffiths
 
c. Consideration of award of contract #F19-10-009 for Psychiatric Services for our Navajo County
Jail to Ellen Morse effective January 1, 2020.  
 
Presented By: Commander Ernie Garcia
 
6. ADMINISTRATIVE SERVICES:  
 
a. Presentation to the Navajo County Finance team for receiving the Certificate of Achievement for
Excellence in Financial Reporting. 
 
Presented By: Bryan Layton
 
b. Consideration of award of contract #B19-08-019 Vehicle Replacement Plan to Arizona Motors
Snowflake, Inc., Arizona Chrysler Dodge Jeep Ram Show Low and Show Low Ford.
 
Presented By: Bryan Layton

<!-- page 4 -->
7. ASSESSOR:  
 
a. PUBLIC HEARING: Consideration and possible adoption of Resolution Number 32-19,
approving the Revised Fee Schedule for the Navajo County Assessor's Office.  
 
Presented By: Cammy Darris
 
8. PUBLIC WORKS:  
 
a. PUBLIC HEARING: Consideration and possible adoption of Resolution Number 33-19 
approving/denying a Zone Change Request from the existing S.D. (Special Development)
Single Family zoning on a 127.2 acre parcel known as "Silver Creek Home Sites" within the
White Mountain Lakes Conceptual Master Plan to 125.8 acres of R-3 (Multiple-Family
Residential) to allow them to develop an RV subdivision and 1.34 acres of
C-R (Commercial-Residential) zoning on parcel APN 304-11-045 and 304-78-001B, a portion
of Township 11 North, Range 22 East, Sections 9 and 10 in the White Mountain Lake area.
 
Presented By: Sandra Phillips
 
b. PUBLIC HEARING: Consideration and adoption of Resolution Number 34-19
approving/denying a Special Use Permit allowing for the construction of approximately 3,650
acre, 477 MW wind energy generation and storage facility on parcels that are zoned A-General
or RU-1, APN 110-01-004, & 110-01-005, portions of Township 15 North, Range 15 East,
Section 22, 26, 27, 34, 35 and 36 in the Chevelon Canyon area.
 
Presented By: Sandra Phillips & Cody Cooper
 
c. PUBLIC HEARING: Consideration and adoption of Resolution Number 35-19,
approving/denying the request for a Special Use Permit to operate a custom fabrication and
repair welding shop in an existing building, which originally was the Timber Mesa Fire Station
on parcel APN 212-10-051, a portion of Township 9 North, Range 22 East, Section 9 in the
Wagon Wheel area.
 
Presented By: Sandra Phillips
 
d. PUBLIC HEARING: Consideration and possible adoption of Resolution Number 36-19,
approving/denying the request to amend Site Plan of Boulders RV and Mobile Home Park,
previously approved by the Board through Resolution #19-94, to replace 2 manufactured home
lots with 6 RV lots on parcel APN 207-16-047F, a portion of Township 12 North, Range 16
East, Section 23 in the Heber area.
 
Presented By: Sandra Phillips
 
e. PUBLIC HEARING: Consideration and possible adoption of Resolution Number 37-19,
approving/denying the request to approve the Special Use Permit to allow a RV Park with
storage on APN 206-34-004C, Township 12 North, Range 17 East, Section 20 of the Gila and
Salt River Meridian in the Heber Area
 
Presented By: Sandra Phillips
 
9. BOARD OF SUPERVISORS:  
 
a. Presentation to retiring employee Delton Jenkins (Facilities Management) for his 33+ years of
service to Navajo County.
 
Presented By: Eric Scott/Bret Starns

<!-- page 5 -->
b. Swearing in of Daryl Seymore as Navajo County Board of Supervisor District IV effective
December 16, 2019.
 
Presented By: Honorable Ralph Hatch
 
c. Presentation to Supervisor Steve Williams for his service to Navajo County.  
Presented By: Board of Supervisors 
 
10. COUNTY BUSINESS UPDATE: Report from County Manager, County Attorney and Board
members.
 
 
11. ADJOURN  
 
Dated: December 6, 2019 NAVAJO COUNTY BOARD OF SUPERVISORS 
Posted: 11:45 a.m. By: MB                         
Melissa W. Buckley - Clerk of the Board

Board of Supervisors Regular 2. g.        
Meeting Date: 12/10/2019  
Title: Name an unnamed road in the Heber area to "Spotted Saddle Trail"
Submitted For: John Osgood, Public Works Director 
Submitted By: Julianna Davis, GIS/E911 Addressing/Row Analyst
Department: Public Works
Motion before the Board:
Name an existing unnamed road in the Heber area as "Spotted Saddle Trail" in Section 30,
Township 12 North, Range 17 East 
Background:
The road is in Section 30, Township 12 North - Range 17 East. (See attached maps) Map
6-11 and Survey 2018-4807. This road currently serves 6 properties and is not County
maintained.  In order to effectively address for E911 emergency service response, an
access should be named when 3 or more property owners use the same access.
A letter and opinion survey were mailed out to 4 property owners who are adjacent to the
road. One was neutral to the naming of the road. One in support of the naming (one
property owner currently owns 3 parcels). Two were opposed of the naming. This resulted
in 3 properties in support of the address change, 2 properties opposed, and 1 neutral, or
66.7% of the properties either in support or neutral.
 
During the past year, staff has worked with the property owners to achieve consensus on
the naming of the road.  In response to the property owner who recommended another
name, staff sent out a  Petition to Name a Road to have property owners propose another
name. No agreement has been reached. Given there has been no response in approximately
three months and staff is not aware of any hardship to property owners arising from the
name change, staff recommends naming the unnamed road Spotted Saddle Road and
believes the E-911 emergency response improvement is in the best interest of the County. 
Fiscal Impact
Fiscal Year: 2019
Budgeted Y/N: N
Amount Requested:
Fiscal Impact:
No Fiscal Impact is expected.

Title: IGA with Cities for Byrne Grant
Submitted For: David Clouse, Sheriff  Submitted By: Cheryl Powell, Deputy Chief

Motion before the Board:
Intergovernmental Agreement between the Sheriff's Office and cities of Winslow and Show Low
and Towns of Snowflake and Taylor regarding FY20 Byrne grant funding
Background:
The Major Crimes Apprehension Team (MCAT) is composed of participants from the Sheriff's
Office and the cities of Winslow and Show Low and Town of Snowflake-Taylor.  This IGA
outlines the approximate amount that each of the participating cities will be reimbursed to
partially fund their detective position.  For FY 20 the approximate amount is $40,000 per
detective.  They are reimbursed upon receipt of a quarterly invoice and back up documentation.
The cities also agree to comply with the terms/conditions of the Byrne grant DC-20-009.

Board of Supervisors Regular 2. l.        
Meeting Date: 12/10/2019  
Title: Request for ARRF Funds for Bullying Campaign
Submitted For: Brad Carlyon, County Attorney 
Submitted By: Maxine Tyler, Executive Assistant
Department: County Attorney
Motion before the Board:
ARRF Request for Holbrook Junior High School Anti-Bullying Campaign reimbursement not to
exceed $250.00
Background:
Ellie Cazee went to her junior high principal, Dr. Jeri McKinnon, and asked if she could put on an
anti-bullying campaign.  She felt students needed to be aware of bullying, notice it, and stand up
to it, and have a better understanding of how it feels to be bullied, and realize it has long-lasting
effects.  One of the activities is "Do-nut" bully.  There will be a kick off speech and each student
will get a donut, along with completing a 3-question survey about bullying.  Survey results will be
reported back to the students as well as, at the end of the week, having the students pledge to not
bully, be aware of it, stand up to it, realize how it feels and acknowledge it can leave scars.

Title: Request to Approve Legal Representation by the Attorney General's Office in 2020
Tax Appeals
Submitted For: Jason Moore, Deputy County Attorney 
Submitted By: Jason Moore, Deputy County Attorney
Department: County Attorney
Motion before the Board:
Legal representation of Navajo County by the Arizona Attorney General's Office in appeals for
tax year 2020 in Centurylink Corp. v. ADOR & Navajo County et. al.,  TX-2019-001726, and
Transwestern v. ADOR & Navajo County et. al., TX-2019-001725
Background:
The County Attorney's Office seeks Board of Supervisors approval of legal representation of the
County by the Arizona Attorney General's Office in these two new tax appeals that have been
filed for tax year 2020.   Both of these appeals concern property that is, under Arizona law,
centrally assessed by the Arizona Department of Revenue rather than the County Assessor. 
Navajo County is named as a party in these matters only because the County collects taxes on the
properties in question and could be liable for a refund of taxes if the Plaintiff is successful.  It is
standard practice for the Attorney General's Office to represent the counties in matters involving
centrally assessed properties.

Board of Supervisors Regular 2. n.        
Meeting Date: 12/10/2019  
Title: ASLD Right-of-Way Aquisition Agreement with Gateway Oasis IV LLC
Submitted For: John Osgood, Public Works Director 
Submitted By: Bryan Cook, Sr. Engineering Project Manager II
Department: Public Works
Motion before the Board:
Agreement with Gateway Oasis IV LLC for transitioning and acquiring a public easement from
the Arizona State Land Department
Background:
Navajo County was approached by Gateway Oasis IV LLC to transition a Right-of-Way (ROW)
acquisition application with the Arizona State Land Department held by Gateway Oasis IV LLC
to Navajo County so that the ROW can be dedicated perpetually to the Public.  This option is not
available otherwise.  
This agreement formalizes the requirements and role each agency will fulfill. Navajo County will
be acting as administrators only in this acquisition where all fees, costs, or development
requirements will be passed on to Gateway Oasis IV LLC.
If approved, this collaboration will result in a Public ROW that can be utilized by Gateway Oasis
IV LLC to file and complete a subdivision in the White Mountain Lake Community Area. All
other requirements for this subdivision will be associated with Planning and Zoning processes.
If not approved, Gateway Oasis can only apply for a 10 year term ROW that would then need to
be re-authorized every 10 years creating a potential issue for the planned subdivision regarding
guaranteed permanent access.
 
Fiscal Impact
Fiscal Year: 2019
Budgeted Y/N: N
Amount Requested: $0
Fiscal Impact:
No fiscal impact is expected.

CERTIFICATION STATEMENT 
 
 
The Navajo County Board of Supervisors hereby certifies that, pursuant to A.R.S. § 41-
2421 C: 
 
1. Navajo County collects certain monies from the Superior Court, including the Clerk 
of the Court, Justice Courts Precincts, # 1, #2, #3, #4, #5, and #6 in Navajo County 
for the payment of filing fees, including clerk fees, diversion fees, adult and 
juvenile probation fees, juvenile monetary assessments, fines, penalties, 
surcharges, sanctions and forfeitur es (with the exception of the Clean Elections 
Fund 10% surcharge, restitution, child support and bonds); and

collections; and

comply with the Fill the Gap legislation in A.R.S.  41 -2421 C; and 
 
5. The total of the collections during FY2016-2017 allocable to the 5% “set aside”  
Fill the Gap fund is:  $193,282.03.

NAVAJO COUNTY  
Board of Supervisors 
 
 
  
Lee Jack Sr. • Jesse Thompson •Jason E. Whiting • Steve Williams • Dawnafe Whitesinger  
“We are Navajo County” 
 
 
 
 
Navajo County - For Official Use Only 
 
 
 
November 18, 2019 
 
 
 
Arizona Department of Environmental Quality  
Water Quality Division 
Clean Water Act §404 Roadmap 
1110 W. Washington St. 
Phoenix, Az 85007 
 
Re:  Navajo County comments on the Arizona Department of Environmental Quality Proposed 
 Program Roadmap for the assumption of the Clean Water Act § 404 permitting process  
 
Mr. David Lelsz, 
 
Thank you for reaching out to Navajo County to seek our opinion on the ADEQ Proposed Program 
Roadmap for the State to assume responsibility for the CWA § 404 permitting process. While we 
commend your agency for working to improve turn -around timelines for the processing of 404 
permit reviews and approvals, we cannot support  the additional cost that would be incurred by 
Counties if this proposal is enacted. In your October 16th email to our County Manager you asked 
the question,  “As a valued stakeholder, if you had to pay the fees as described in this Road -map, 
would the proposed program provide enough value for you to support ADEQ's assumption of the 
CWA § 404 program?”  Our answer to this question is, No. We do not support the increased fees. 
We could however support the assumption , if the fees to Counties were limited as w e propose in 
the following paragraph entitled “Remedy”.  
 
The following paragraphs provide addition detail and specifics explaining our position on this 
matter.  
 
While Navajo County generally supports the assumption of federal permitting and compliance 
processes by State agencies, we would like to comment specif ically on one critical issue with the 
ADEQ CWA § 404 Proposed Program Roadmap.  
 
Fee structure 
 
The ADEQ CWA § 404 Proposed Program Roadmap “Program Fee” section (p.14) identifies 14 
permits (32%) that will require a fee under certain threshold conditions, and 20 permits (46%) that 
will always require a fee. 
 
In effect, for 78% of the United States Army Corps of Engineers Preliminary Jurisdictional 
Determination, Approved Jurisdictional Determination, General Permit Authorization and

<!-- page 458 -->
Navajo County - For Official Use Only 
Individual Permit that are applicable in the state program jurisdictional waters, local government 
would now have to pay a substantial fee for the delivery of a permit. 
 
The minimum fee would be $7,875 and the maximum fee would be $54,800 plus a $195 hourly 
review charge. In effect, securing just one individual permit with 80 hours of review and a single 
discharge Approved Jurisdictional Determination would cost local governments $81,275. 
 
In contrast, the current cost to local governments for such a permit issued by the United S tates 
Army Corps of Engineers is $0. 
 
Inability to support the transfer of cost from federal or State government to local 
government 
 
While Navajo County understands that the Arizona Department of Environmental Quality needs 
to establish funding for the performance of the permitting work it seeks to assume from the United 
States Army Corps of Engineers, we cannot support the transfer of yet another financial cost from 
federal or State government to local government. 
 
The budgetary reality is that many rural local governments are already struggling on the verge of 
insolvency, and with the financial impossibility to deliver the services that they are required to 
provide to residents and visitors. 
 
From this perspective, local governments constitute a different  category of clients from 
commercial clients. Commercial clients have the possibility to offset their costs through the price 
they charge for their products and services. Local governments do not. 
 
Remedy 
 
Navajo County suggests that the Arizona Department  of Environmental Quality establish a two -
tier fee structure where local governments would be either charged a nominal administrative fee 
not to exceed $500 per permit, or no fee at all. 
 
In summary, Navajo County does not support the assumption of the Clean Water Act and 404 
permit processing by ADEQ as proposed due to the increased costs that counties would incur. We 
could however support the proposal if the fee structure were modified to limit the fees charged to 
counties and local municipalities. 
 
 
Thank you again for the opportunity to provide input on this important proposed action. 
 
Sincerely, 
 
Dawnafe Whitesinger, Chairwoman 
Navajo County Board of Supervisors

ARIZONA STATEMENT OF CITIZENSHIP
OR ALIEN STATUS FOR STATE PUBLIC BENEFITS
Title IV of the federal Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act of 1996 (the "Act"), 8 U.S.C. § 1621,
provides that, with certain exceptions, only United States citizens, United States non -citizen nationals, non-exempt "qualified
aliens" (and sometimes only particular categories of qualified aliens), nonimmigrant, and certain aliens paroled into the
United States are eligible to receive state, or local public benefits. With certain exceptions, a professional license and
commercial license issued by a State agency is a State public benefit.
Arizona Revised Statutes § 41-1080 requires, in general, that a person applying for a license must submit documentation to
the license agency that satisfactorily demonstrates the applicant's presence in the United States is authorized under federal
law.
Directions: All applicants must complete Sections I, II, and IV. Applicants who are not U.S. citizens or nationals must also
complete Section III.
Submit this completed form and a copy of one or more document(s) from the attached "Evidence of U.S. Citizenship, U.S.
National Status, or Alien Status" with your application for license or renewal.If the document you submit does not contain a
photograph, you must also provide a government issued document that contains your photograph.You must submit
supporting legal documentation (i.e. marriage certificate) if the name on your evidence is not the same as your current
legal name.

Board of Supervisors Regular 5. a.        
Meeting Date: 12/10/2019  
Title: Retirement of K-9 Legend
Submitted For: David Clouse, Sheriff  Submitted By: Cheryl Powell, Deputy Chief 
Department: Sheriff 
Presented By: Chief Deputy Sheriff Randy
Moffitt
Subject:
Presentation on service retirement of K-9 Legend.
Background: 
Police Service Dog Legend started with the Sheriff's Office in April 2015 and has worked for
about 4 1/2 years.  During this time Legend has worked as a narcotics detection canine and patrol
canine.  Those duties included sniffing vehicles on traffic stops, sniffing houses during search
warrants, conducting area and building searches while looking for dangerous criminals,
conducting perimeter support during search warrants and assisting with prisoner control once a
dangerous criminal was placed into custody. 
Legend was assigned to Deputy Daniel Deets and their first day as a team seized 43 pounds of
marijuana.  In just his second week on the job Legend helped safely locate and apprehend a
wanted fugitive hiding under a log in Heber.  Legend has had a very successful career with the
Sheriff's Office helping seize approximately 1,550 pounds of marijuana, 351 pounds of
methamphetamine, 20 pounds of cocaine, 13.5 pounds of heroin, 3 pounds of fentanyl and
$3,373,030 in illegal drug proceeds and assets.  As recently as 2018 Legend's efforts assisted in
taking a violent wanted person into custody without incident.
Legend has a very fun personality and is very photogenic as can be seen on many of the Sheriff's
Office Facebook posts.  He is very social, loves his toy and loves anything to do with playing. 
Legend has truly lived up to his name during his time with the Sheriff's Office and will be sorely
missed.

Board of Supervisors Regular 5. b.        
Meeting Date: 12/10/2019  
Title: Admn Fees for Vehicles Towed for ARS Title 13 Chapter 34 Drug Offenses
Submitted For: David Clouse, Sheriff  Submitted By: Cheryl Powell, Deputy Chief 
Department: Sheriff 
Presented By: Deputy Chief Don Griffiths
Motion before the Board:
PUBLIC HEARING: Consideration and possible adoption of Resolution Number 31-19,
approving the collection of administrative fees for vehicles towed/seized during the investigation
of ARS Title 13, Chapter 34 Drug Offense violations.
Background:
The Sheriff's Office wishes to collect administrative fees related to the vehicles towed/seized
during the investigation of a violation of ARS Title 13, Chapter 34 Drug Offenses. The fees
would consist of one hundred dollars ($100) and an additional storage fee of five dollars ($5) per
day after five (5) days until the date the owner or party having legal interest picks up the vehicle. 
Such storage fees not to exceed five hundred dollars ($500).
The administrative fees would offset the cost of manpower in removing the vehicle from the
scene to the impound lot, collection of evidence contained in the vehicle, inventory of the
vehicle and overseeing and managing the impound lot.
Recommendation: 
Approve Administrative Fees in relation to vehicles towed/seized during the investigation of ARS
Title 13 Chapter 34 Drug Offenses.

(including expenses incurred by the Count y as a result of the Consultant’s 
default), Consultant shall be entitled to  payment for its per formance up to the 
amount of such excess.  If  the cost of finishing the work exceeds the unpaid 
balance, Consultant shall pay the difference to County. 
 
c. Termination for Convenience.  County, by written notice to Consultant, may 
terminate this Agreement in whole or part when in the sole discretion of 
County it is in County’s best interests to do so.  Consultant shall be paid for all 
material, equipment and services provi ded, as well as reasonable termination 
expenses and a reasonable allowance fr om profit and ov erhead, provided 
that such payments, excl usive of termination expens es, shall not exceed the 
total amount payable pursuant to Sect ion 6 less any payments previously 
made to Consultant.  Consultant shall not be entitled to pr ofit and overhead 
on material, equipment and services which were not provided. 
 
d. Consultant’s Responsibility.  Upon receipt of a termination notice, 
Consultant shall (a) promptly disconti nue all services (unless notice directs 
otherwise), and (b) deliver or otherwise make available to County copies of all 
data, reports, summaries and other info rmation and materials developed or 
accumulated by Consultant in performing this Agreement.

<!-- page 500 -->
5 
 
15. Termination by Consultant.  Consultant may terminate this Agreement upon 
written notice to County if performance is made impossible for a period of sixty (60) 
consecutive calendar days for any of the following reasons through no act or fault 
of Consultant or its agents,  employees or subcontractors:  issuance of an order by 
a count or other public author ity having jurisdiction; an ac t of government, such as 
a declaration of national emergency; or a nat ural disaster or other Act of God.  
Consultant may also terminate this Ag reement upon written notice and a ten-day 
opportunity to cure if County fails to ma ke any payment within time set forth in 
Section 6.  Consultant may also termi nate this Agreement upon written notice if 
suspensions, delays or interruptions by  County equal in the aggregate more than 
100% of the total number of days scheduled for completion. 
 
16. Governing Law.  This Agreement shall be governed by the law of the State of 
Arizona.  Any suit arising out of this Agr eement shall be brought in the state courts 
of Arizona (with venue in Na vajo County) or federal Dis trict of Arizona, but only 
after informal negotiation pursuant to Section 13. 
 
17. Incorporation of Applicable Laws.   Every provision of la w required by statute or 
regulation to be in this Agreement will be read and enforced as though included 
herein.  Each party shall promptly notify the other up on discovery that any such 
provision has been omitted. 
 
18. Non-Collusion.  The provisions A.R.S. 38-511 ar e incorporated herein by this 
reference. 
 
19. One-Year Limitation on Actions.  No action shall be maintained by Consultant on 
any claim based upon or arising out of this Agreement unless such action is 
commenced within one year after the County’s final payment hereunder. 
 
20. Entire Agreement.   This Agreement and those documents incorporated by 
reference represent the entire understanding between the parties.  No amendment 
shall be effective unless executed by both parties with the same formality as this 
Agreement.  Provided, however, that t he County’s designated representative is 
authorized to modify the Scope of Work, in writing, with the concurrence of 
Consultant so long as the project is not changed substantially or significant 
additional compensation is not required. 
 
21. Severability.  The provisions of this Agreement are severable.  Any provision held 
to be invalid or unenforceable shall not affe ct the validity or enf orceability of any 
other provision.

Submitted By: Melissa Buckley, Clerk of the Board of Supervisors
Department: Board of Supervisors
Presented By: Bryan Layton
Subject:
Presentation to the Navajo County Finance team for receiving the Certificate of Achievement for
Excellence in Financial Reporting. 
Background: 
The Navajo County Finance team has received the Certificate of Achievement for Excellence in
Financial Reporting by the Government Finance Officers Association of the United States and
Canada for its comprehensive annual financial report. The Certificate of Achievement is the
highest form of recognition in the area of governmental accounting and financial reporting, and its
attainment represents a significant accomplishment by a government and its management.

Board of Supervisors Regular 6. b.        
Meeting Date: 12/10/2019  
Title: Award of Contract B19-08-019 Vehicle Replacement Plan
Submitted For: Bryan Layton, Assistant County Manager 
Submitted By: Jeanine Carruthers, Deputy Director Administration
Department: Administrative Services
Presented By: Bryan Layton
Motion before the Board:
Consideration of award of contract #B19-08-019 Vehicle Replacement Plan to Arizona Motors
Snowflake, Inc., Arizona Chrysler Dodge Jeep Ram Show Low and Show Low Ford.
Background:
Sealed proposals were received by the Board of Supervisors at the Navajo County Governmental
Center, Holbrook, Arizona until 2:00 p.m. M.S.T, November 20, 2019, in strict accordance with
the specifications on file in the office of the Navajo County Public Works.  No bids were accepted
after 2:00 p.m. M.S.T.  The bids were publicly opened and read aloud at 2:15 p.m.  This is a
annual "multi-award" contract for Navajo County's Vehicle Replacement Plan which allows
vehicles to be purchased based on price, convenience, availability and/or quality.  The award of
contracts to all bidders allows adequate coverage for vehicle purchases throughout the year on an
"as needed" basis.
CONTRACT HIGHLIGHTS:
1. Contract will be on a “as needed basis”.
2. Annual contract subject to renewal up to 4 additional one-year terms.
3. Multiple award – in whole or in part, by item or group of items, by section or geographic
area, or make multiple awards, where such action serves the County’s best interest.
4. Bidders may bid on all items and groups. Bidding $0.00 or leaving a blank space in the
unit price or extended price column shall render the item so bid non-responsive, but
shall in no way invalidate the remaining items.
5. Price’s may be adjusted via an amendment approved by the Board of Supervisors for
new production years.
6. Estimated quantities 10-20 vehicles per fiscal year.
OPTIONAL – the following items are optional and are not considered in the evaluation of
responses to this solicitation:
1. Cooperative Purchasing – all vendors have indicated that other public agencies may
purchase off of the contract during the contract term.
2. Voluntary Employee Discounts – all vendors have indicated that they will provide
voluntarily discounts to County
employees - list to be provided at a later date.

Staff recommends award of contracts as presented.

zoning on parcel APN 304-11-045 and 304-78-001B, a portion of Township 11 North, Range 22
East, Sections 9 and 10 in the White Mountain Lake area.
Background:
The subject property has been part of previous zone changes and master plans.  The most recent
and relevant Conceptual Master Site Plan was approved in 2006 by the Board of Supervisors in
Resolution #83-06.  These properties were a portion of the Silver Creek Home Sites which was
intended to be single family residential in nature with a density of 1.57 dwelling units per acre.
The project is approximately 1/4 mile from Juniper Ridge and Silver Creek Village which are both
multi-family developments, separated from the project by a segment of State Land.
Staff initially requested that the applicant amend the existing Conceptual Master Site Plan to
reflect their desire to construct an RV subdivision that would allow the property owner to lease or
sell the lots.  However the applicant does not control the remaining portion of the Board-approved
Master Plan that is undeveloped, so is unable to transfer density from a property they do not own
or control to their property.
This item was heard at the November 21, 2019 meeting of the Planning and Zoning Commission. 
Several White Mountain Lake area residents spoke in opposition to the project, citing concerns of
reduced property values, increased traffic, and crime.  Related to the concerns of increased traffic,
a condition of approval recommended by the Commission and staff is that a traffic impact study
be completed, and if existing street facilities are not adequate for the proposed
development resulting from this Zone Change, the developer shall pay for off-site
improvements.  The Planning and Zoning Commission uanimously recommended
approval of the zone change to the Board of Supervisors.

Recommendation: 
Planning & Zoning Commission and Staff recommends approval of this Zone Change with the
condition that off-site roadway improvements may need to be made, pending a Traffic Impact
Study during the development phase of the project.

BACKGROUND: 
 
The properties referred to within this report have been subject to a number of Zone Changes and Conceptual 
Master Plans throughout the history of Navajo County.  The most recent, and relevant, Conceptual Master 
Site Plan was approved in 2006 through Board of Supervisors Resolution #83-06.  This Resolution was 
approved with the following condition: 
 
1. All technical requirements of the Subdivision Regulations and Requirements, Flood Control 
Ordinance, Building Safety Ordinance and applicable codes shall be adhered to and approved at the 
proper Tentative Plat, Final Plat or Building Permit and construction phase (to include, without 
limitation, the Traffic Impact Analysis, Flood Plain Study, Drainage Study, Construction 
Improvement Plans and Grading Plans. 
 
The 2006 Conceptual Master Site Plan, of which these properties were a part, contained a Master 
Development Plan for the entirety of the White Mountain Lake area.  These properties were a portion of the 
Silver Creek Home Sites which was intended to be single-family residential in nature.  This section of the 
Master Development Plan was designed to have 603 units over an area of 383 acres. 
 
The subject property is located approximately one-quarter mile from Juniper Ridge and Silver Creek 
Village, both of which are multi-family developments that have been completed in the area.  The only 
reason this property is separated from the other two multi-family developments is the fact that there is a 
small portion of State Land to the north of White Mountain Lake Road.  The majority of properties nearby to 
these parcels are zoned some form of Special Development or Rural 1 (1 Acre Per Dwelling Unit). 
 
ZONING DISTRICTS: 
 
ARTICLE 17 – SPECIAL DEVELOPMENT ZONE 
 
Section 1701 – Purpose.  
 
1. The purpose of the Special Development zone is to provide for the development of subdivisio ns 
and other land use projects containing various dwelling types, necessary commercial centers, off 
street parking areas, open space areas for recreation, and to preserve a rural atmosphere. 
 
2. Deviations from design standards for the specific zone or zones may be permitted provided open 
spaces are developed and maintained for the use of the residents and provided further that the 
parcel size, soil conditions, terrain, ground cover and other significant natural features favor this 
type of development. 
 
ARTICLE 14 – (R-3) MULTIPLE-FAMILY RESIDENTIAL ZONING DISTRICT  
 
Section 1401 – Purpose. 
 
The principal purpose of this zoning district is to provide for multiple-family housing along with certain 
transient residential and on -residential neighborhoods in locations which are s uitable and appropriate 
taking into consideration existing conditions, including present use of land, future land use needs and 
the availability of public utilities.  The minimum parcel size required is six thousand (6,000) square feet 
in area and the mini mum area required for each dwelling unit is one thousand (1,000) square feet.  
Principal uses permitted in this zoning district include high-density housing, hospitals, and institutio ns

<!-- page 534 -->
of an educational, religious, charitable or philanthropic nature, private clubs and fraternal organizatio ns, 
resort hotels, Manufactured home subdivisions and Manufactured Home Parks. 
 
COMPREHENSIVE PLAN/AREA PLAN:  
 
Comprehensive Plan 
 
4.0 Land Use Element 
 
 4.4 Character Areas and Overlay 
 
 4.4.4 Community Village 
 
The purpose of the Community Village character area is to provide large areas with higher 
density residential development with a mix of related commercial, industrial and institutio nal 
uses extending from highway corridors and highway intersections.  Commu nity Village is an 
appropriate and encouraged location for uses such as community college campuses and hospitals 
or medical clinics.   
 
All “subdivision” development in Community Village should have paved access.  Residential 
“subdivision” development has no maximum or minimum density requirement. 
 
4.7 Goals and Policies 
 
Goal 2: To administer the Land Use Element of the Navajo County Comprehensive Plan so as to 
further the purposes of the Plan. 
 
 Policy 2-A: Approve zone changes that are consistent with the Land Use Element’s character 
 areas, as shown on the Land Use Map.  However, the Land Use Element and Map shall not be 
 used as the sole justification for making decisions on zone changes. 
 
- The Community Village character area, which is applicable to the subject properties, 
encourages providing higher density residential development with a mix of commercial and 
other uses, for which this Zone Change would allow. 
 
Goal 9: Actively plan to accommodate growth in Navajo County in an appropriate manner. 
 
Policy 9-B: Encourage higher density and intensity development in those areas of the County 
where services, including, but not limited to, water and sewer systems, paved rights-of-way, and 
schools, are available or can be created with new development. 
 
- The area in the vicinity of this proposal has access to water, sewer systems, and nearby right-
of-way, though all of these components may require improvements depending on the type 
of subdivision or development proposed.  
 
5.0 Circulation Element 
 
5.4 Goals and Policies 
 
Goal 4: Provide for safe travel and access to property.

<!-- page 535 -->
Policy 4 -G: Approve subdivisions and rezonings  only where existing street facilities are 
adequate or where the developer agrees to pay for off -site improvements necessitated by the 
proposed development.  Consider adoption of either a development fee program that would 
provide credits for such off-site improvements or another financing mechanism to reimburse a 
developer for a portion of its expenses when later development occurs that benefits from the 
improvements. 
 
ANALYSIS: 
 
There are a number of factors that should be considered in the evaluation of this proposed Zone 
Change.  The first is the appropriateness of multi-family residential zoning within this general area.  
Most recently, this land was approved for medium to high-density single-family residential through a 
Master Development Plan.  Despite this designation, due to the location and infrastructure in place, 
the Comprehensive Plan and subject Character Area support a Zone Change to a higher density 
designation.  With the infrastructure, depending on the proposal, it will be important to note that any 
developers will need to pay for the necessary cost of improvements to keep said infrastructure 
adequate.  
 
Within the general vicinity of these properties are a number of high-density developments that have 
been approved in the past, both single and multi-family residential.  The two multi-family residential 
developments of note are Juniper Ridge and Silver Creek Village, which are only separated from the 
subject properties by State Land. 
 
Due to the fact that this proposal meets the goals of the Comprehensive Plan and subject Character 
Area as well as the fact that there are multi-family residential developments in close vicinity to this 
proposal, Planning and Zoning Staff supports the requested Zone Change from Special Development 
to R-3 (Multiple Family Residential Zoning District). 
 
A public meeting was held on August 23rd, 2019 at the Holiday Inn Express conference room in Show 
Low as required by State law.  At this meeting, there were 64 attendees that signed in, with a number 
choosing to forego this step.  The majority of concerns raised at this meeting were over usage and 
issues with a development in relation to White Mountain Lake and inadequate infrastructure.  
Considerations regarding White Mountain Lake are outside of the purview of Navajo County Planning 
and Zoning as this is a privately-owned lake.  As far as infrastructure, staff and the applicant are aware 
that there will likely need to be improvements and updates to roads, water, and sewer, for which the 
applicant will be responsible.  These improvements will need to be addressed if a subdivision or 
development is approved for the subject properties. 
 
At the Planning and Zoning Commission Hearing held on Thursday, November 21 st, Planning and 
Zoning Staff made the recommendation of approval, subject to the conditions outlined in this report.  
The Planning and Zoning Commission unanimously voted to recommend approval of this item subject 
to the same conditions recommended by Staff. 
 
At the Planning and Zoning Commission Hearing held on Thursday, November 21st, Planning and 
Zoning Staff made the recommendation of approval of the Zone Change, subject to a condition related 
to infrastructure improvements.  The Planning and Zoning Commission made the recommendation of 
approval of the Zone Change to the Navajo County Board of Supervisors, subject to an alteration of 
the recommended condition given by Staff.  This altered, recommended condition is contained within 
this report.

INTRODUCTION 
 
The purpose of this narrative is to provide information regarding the re-zoning to a portion of the 
property around White Mountain Lake in Navajo County, Arizona. The site is a portion of an 
existing Master Site Plan. The existing Master Development Plan is comprised of approximately 
1,223.6 acres. The rezone site area is approximately 127.09 acres. The site is located northwest 
of White Mountain Lake. The purpose of the rezone is to provide an RV/Park Model development 
that utilizes open space to provide a rural development in the area. The project will provide RV 
rental sites on both a short term and long-term basis. There will potentially be some park model 
homes for longer term rental as well. The development will highlight Silver Creek, which flows 
through the site and will also provide amenities such as a store, showers and Club House. The 
development is also planned to have some areas for overnight camping. The development will 
also be part of the recreation district that utilizes White Mountain Lake. The purpose of the rezone 
will be to provide R-3 zoning for a majority of the site and a small portion will be C-R for a small 
store at the entrance.

DRAINAGE 
 
Typically, storm water enters the site from four (4) different areas. There is water that flows from 
the outlet of White Mountain Lake, under the dam and down the Silver Creek. This is a 
controlled outlet. When Mexican Lake (located north of White Mountain Lake) fills and 
overflows, the overflow will enter Silver Creek from the east side. And there are two drainage 
areas on each side of Silver Creek (west and east drainage areas) that flow to the site from 
offsite. Figure 9 indicates these four areas and delineates the two offsite flow areas. The figure 
generally indicates the flow directions with black arrows. All these flows make their way to the 
Silver Creek and then downstream of the site. The flows out of White Mountain Lake and 
Mexican Lake will continue to flow directly to the creek. The west and east drainage areas will 
flow through the site. The site will be designed to utilize culverts and channels to convey the 
offsite storm waters through the site and to Silver Creek, where the storm water will be 
contained in the canyon and will be conveyed off the site.

SEWER 
 
The site is just south of an existing wastewater treatment facility. The facility is owned by White 
Mountain Lake Sanitation, Incorporated (Sewer Company). The Sewer Company has an 
existing gravity sewer line that is located across the existing White Mountain Lake dam and 
continues northward in the existing abandoned railroad grade to the treatment plant. The 
existing sewer line crosses onto the site just south of the treatment plant. Based on 
conversations with the owner of the Sewer Company, this existing line can be connected into 
providing sewer to the project. 
 
 
Figure 12. EXISTING SEWER MAP

<!-- page 558 -->
Site Plan Narrative  Gateway Oasis 
14 | P a g e 
 
The sewer treatment plant has an existing lease boundary that generally extends north and 
west of the treatment plant. As can be seen on Figure 12, the lease boundary is outside the 
project site. 
 
The sewer treatment plant treats the influent from the sewer system and then re-uses the 
treated effluent by sprinkling the effluent on a portion of the reuse area. The Sewer Company 
provided information regarding the requirements of the Aquifer Protection Permit for the sewer 
treatment plant and the reuse area of the plan. The treatment plant itself is capable of treating 
250,000 gallons per day (gpd). The reuse area has three (3) different phases. Each phase has a 
“trigger point” in flows in gpd in which the operator must move to the next phase. The maximum 
flows for each phase are indicated in Table 1 below. 
 
Table 1. Reuse Flow Rates 
PHASE MAXIMIMUM FLOW RATE 
Phase 1 20,000 gpd 
Phase 2 62,000 gpd 
Phase 3 125,000 gpd 
 
When the maximum flows are reached, the sprinkler system will have to be expanded to reuse 
more effluent. This also will require some fencing expansion as well as some berms being 
constructed to contain the reuse water to ensure it stays on the site. It was indicated that the 
treatment plant is currently receiving flows real close to the 20,000 gpd that will require the 
expansion to the Phase 2 reuse area. Therefore, this project will definitely put the flows over 
that threshold if it doesn’t happen before the development is connected to the system. 
 
The entire project will have 748 lots, with 200 in Phase 1. The remainder will be in Phase 2. The 
sewer flows from the development were estimated using Table 1 from AAC R18-9-E323. The 
population was determined assuming 2.7 people per lot and using 80 gallons per person per 
day from Table 1. The results are indicated in Table 2 below. 
 
Table 2. Estimated Sewer Flows 
PHASE # OF UNITS ESTIMATED 
POPULATION 
ESTIMATED SEWER 
FLOWS (GPD) 
Phase 1 200 540 43,200 
Phase 2 100 270 21,600 
Total 300 810 64,800 
 
Based on these estimations, Phase 1 will put the daily flows over the Phase 1 threshold of 
20,000 gpd and may also put the flows to the treatment plant over the Phase 2 threshold of 
62,000 gpd when the lots are full. An agreement will have to be made with the Sewer Company 
as to how they will be compensated to expand the reuse area. Expansion will have to be 
considered for Phase 2. 
 
Because of the terrain of the site, sewer lift stations will be required to get the sewer to the 
existing sewer main that leads to the sewer treatment plant. These will be part of the detailed 
design of the sewer system for the project.

Traffic to the development will enter the site on the south end near the White Mountain Lake

COMPREHENSIVE PLAN 
 
As part of Navajo County’s Comprehensive Plan, a Character Areas (Exhibit 2, Comprehensive

Character Areas Map that was obtained from the Navajo County website is shown in Figure 14,

The brown portion that the site is in is designated as having a Character Area of “Community 
Village” as indicated in Navajo County’s Comprehensive Plan, dated May 24, 2011. Character 
Areas in the plan represent generalized land use, development, or preservation concepts, as 
indicated by the Comprehensive Plan. Character Areas designate more general uses for areas of 
the County than zoning. 
The Comprehensive Plan indicates the following: 
“The purpose of the Community Village character area is to provide large areas with 
higher density residential development with a mix of related commercial, industrial and 
institutional uses extending from highway corridors and highway intersections. 
Community Village is an appropriate and encouraged location for uses such as 
community college campuses and hospitals or medical clinics.” (Section 4.4.4, 
Comprehensive Plan) 
This development fits the Community Village character area. Section 4.4.4 of the Comprehensive 
Plan indicates that Community Village can be a mix of residential and commercial and has no 
maximum or minimum density.  
SITE

<!-- page 561 -->
Site Plan Narrative  Gateway Oasis 
17 | P a g e 
 
OPEN SPACE 
 
Most of the open space for the Gateway Oasis White Mountain Lake development will be 
located along the Silver Creek. The Silver Creek is a great amenity that is located on the 
property and the owner would like to feature the creek and provide recreational access all along 
the creek on the entire property. Additional areas of open space will be provided throughout the 
project. Figure 15 below indicates the general location of open space for the project. The green 
and blue areas are planned to be open space. 
 
 
Figure 15. OPEN SPACE MAP 
 Calculations were completed to estimate the amount of open space for the project. The project 
will have 70.90 acres of open space. The total project size is 127.09 acres. This provides 55.8% 
open space for the project.

<!-- page 562 -->
Site Plan Narrative  Gateway Oasis 
18 | P a g e 
 
AMENITIES 
The project will have several amenities which will make the project attractive to many different 
lifestyles. A list of the amenities planned for the project are listed below. 
 Silver Creek 
 Trails 
 White Mountain Lake 
 Store 
 Clubhouse 
 Swimming Pool 
 Showers/Laundry Facilities 
 
 
SILVER CREEK 
The Silver Creeks exits White Mountain Lake Dam and flows directly through the project site. 
Along the creek is a relatively vast amount of vegetation and therefore wildlife that is fed by the 
water from the creek. The creek is located in the bottom of a rock canyon that will provide 
serenity and views for people in the area. 
 
TRAILS 
There is an existing well-traveled trail that travels along the Silver Creek in the bottom of the 
canyon. This existing trail along the creek will be the highlight of the trail system for the 
development. New trails will be constructed along the roadways with connection points down to 
the trail along the creek, providing unique opportunities for a place to walk in the area. 
 
WHITE MOUNTIAN LAKE 
A portion of the project is in the existing White Mountain Lake Recreation District. The owner 
plans to take advantage of this amenity and provide an opportunity for guests to recreate at the 
White Mountain Lake. The lake provides fishing, water skiing, swimming and has picnic tables 
along the shore.  
 
STORE 
A store will be constructed near the entrance of the development. The store will provide an 
opportunity to stay in the area to purchase food, refreshment and other necessary items. The 
store will be a convenient place to buy commonly needed items without leaving the 
development. 
 
CLUBHOUSE 
A clubhouse will be constructed as part of the project. It will provide a place to have large 
gatherings and perform other activities. 
 
SWIMMING POOL 
Along with the clubhouse will be a swimming pool. The swimming pool will provide a convenient 
location to cool off in the summer months and a place to leisurely enjoy the warm sun. 
 
SHOWERS/LAUNDRY FACILITIES 
Part of the construction will include several buildings providing showers and laundry facilities for 
guests to use when they stay at the site.

<!-- page 563 -->
Site Plan Narrative  Gateway Oasis 
19 | P a g e 
 
RECREATION DISTRICT 
 
The southern portion of the project is currently in the White Mountain Lake Recreational 
District, allowing access and use of White Mountain Lake. The owner would like to utilize 
this allowance and provide use to some of the renters in the project. Property owners in the 
area and current members of the Recreation District have voiced concern that there are 
times when the parking lot for the lake and lake use in general is very high and the area is 
very crowded. The owner has expressed a willingness to discuss the current conditions of 
the lake and possibly expanding the parking area, or additional picnic areas or other things 
that may alleviate some of the crowded areas of the lake. The owner plans to meet with 
members of the organization to see if an agreement can be made. The owner does not plan 
to attempt to annex additional property into the District. 
 
NEIGHBORHOOD MEETING 
 
On August 23, 2019 a “Neighborhood Meeting” was held at the Holiday Inn Express 
conference room in Show Low, Arizona. The meeting was held to inform people in the area 
about the project and let them provide feedback on the development. Navajo County 
provided parcel owner names and addresses for all properties within 500 feet of the project 
boundaries. A sign-in sheet was provided at the meeting in which 64 people signed in. It is 
likely there were others at the meeting that didn’t sign in. The main concerns at the meeting 
were the effects that the addition of the development on the existing water, sewer and 
paving infrastructure as well as the additional people using the lake.  
 
It was explained that as the project moves along in the approval process, the existing water 
system, sewer system and access roads to the site will be examined to determine their 
capability to handle the additional demands on the infrastructure.  
 
It was also explained that the owners of the property have been paying taxes to the 
recreational district for many years. It was also explained that one of the items included with 
the purchase of the property was a right to use the lake, just like all the others property 
purchases within the district. It was explained that the owner does want to have access for 
some of the renters, however the owner does not desire to try and annex more property into 
the district.

Board of Supervisors Regular 8. b.        
Meeting Date: 12/10/2019  
Title: Chevelon Butte Wind Farm
Submitted For: John Osgood, Public Works Director 
Submitted By: Sandra Phillips, Assistant County Engineer/Flood Control Manager
Department: Public Works Division: Planning & Zoning
Presented By: Sandra Phillips & Cody Cooper
Motion before the Board:
PUBLIC HEARING: Consideration and adoption of Resolution Number 34-19
approving/denying a Special Use Permit allowing for the construction of approximately 3,650
acre, 477 MW wind energy generation and storage facility on parcels that are zoned A-General or
RU-1, APN 110-01-004, & 110-01-005, portions of Township 15 North, Range 15 East, Section
22, 26, 27, 34, 35 and 36 in the Chevelon Canyon area.
Background:
The applicant is requesting a Special Use Permit allowing for the construction of a wind energy
generation and storage facility 18 miles south of Winslow, where Highway 99 crosses into
Coconino County.  The proposed project is set to span approximately 3,650 acres in Navajo
County and produce approximately 477 MW of electricity through the entire project.  The
majority of the project is located within Coconino County jurisdiction.  The project is anticipated
to be composed of 164 wind turbines total, of which only 8 turbines will be located within Navajo
County.  The proposed turbine model will range in height from approximately 591 feet to 755 feet. 
The components planned to be constructed in Navajo County including the 8 turbine sites and the
associated collector lines, 3 miles of the 345 kV generation-tie transmission line, the switching
station and interconnection with the existing APS line, and access roads.
The applicant has provided copies of significant impact studies to wildlife and the environment as
well as visualizations and sound analysis.  Please see attached narrative.
The proposed use would be permitted in the zoning by approval of a Special Use Permit. 
Planning & Zoning Commission recommended approval to the Board by a vote of 3 yeas and 2
nay.
Recommendation: 
The Planning and Zoning Commission has recommended the approval of this Special Use Permit
to the Navajo County Board of Supervisors, subject to the conditions in the attached resolution by
a vote of 3-2.  The applicant has reviewed the conditions, and has agreed to them.

NAVAJO N  
NAVAJO COUNTY PUBLIC WORKS DEPARTMENT 
PLANNING & ZONING 
 
 
STAFF REPORT  
BOARD OF SUPERVISORS 
 
Hearing Date: December 10, 2019 
Case No:  19-83 
Action:   Special Use Permit  
Applicant/Owner: Chevelon Butte RE LLC  
Project Name: Chevelon Butte Wind Farm 
PARCEL INFORMATION  
 Address: No Address 
 
 APN:  110-01-004 & 110-01-005 
 
 Legal Desc: Township 15 North, Range 15 East, Sections 22, 26, 27, 34, 35, and 36 of the 
  Gila and Salt River Meridian in the Chevelon Canyon area. 
 
 District: II 
 
 Area:  Chevelon Canyon 
 
 Parcel Size: Approximately 3,650 acres in total. 
 
STATED REASON FOR REQUEST:  
Chevelon Butte RE LLC has requested a Special Use Permit to allow them to construct and operate a 
portion of a 477 MW maximum capacity wind generation facility. 
 
GENERAL CHARACTER OF NEIGHBORHOOD:  
 
Generally, land in the vicinity of the project is either zoned A-General or is Hopi Tribal or State Land, 
which are considered under the RU-1 zoning category in Navajo County for planning purposes.   The 
surrounding land is currently vacant/agricultural. The subject properties are also curr ently vacant and 
being used predominately for livestock grazing and recreation, including hunting.  The nearest legally 
classified residence is approximately ½ mile from the clos est project boundary.  The applicant has 
indicated their nearest wind turbine to a legally classified residence is expected to be 2 ½ miles away.

<!-- page 569 -->
PROJECT DESCRIPTION:  
 
The overall proposed project is a 477 megawatt (MW) maximum nameplate capacity wind energy 
generation facility.  This project is projected to span approximately 3,650 acres in Navajo County and 
37,977 acres in Coconino County.  The proposed infrastructure footprint within the project boundaries 
on the Navajo County side will occupy approximately 58 acres.  On the Navajo County side, the project 
will be located approximately 18 miles south of Winslow in the Chevelon Canyon area. 
 
The entire wind farm is expected to be composed of 164 wind turbine sites.   Of these, only eight (8) 
turbine sites are proposed to be within the Navajo County boundary.  The p roposed turbine models 
range in total height from approximately 591 feet to 755 feet.  The applicant has indicated that they do 
not intend to identify their turbine model until the time of dealing with their Building Permit 
applications.  
 
The project’s other components will include collector lines associated with the wind turbines, up to six 
permanent meteorological towers, two collector substations, and an approximately 12 -mile-long 345 -
kilovolt (kV) generation tie transmission line, an interconnection sw itching station, an operations and 
maintenance building and laydown yard, and access roads. 
 
Of the above, the components planned to be constructed in Navajo County are up to eight turbine sites 
and their associated collector lines, 3 miles of the 345-kV generation-tie transmission line, the switching 
station and interconnection with the existing APS line, and access roads. 
 
Access to the switching station from the Navajo County side is proposed to be across Hutch Road and 
existing U.S. Forest Service roads coming out of the Heber/Overgaard area.   During the constructio n 
period, access for delivery, construction and maintenance of all infrastructure west of Chevelon Canyon 
of will be from State Route 99 in Coconino County. 
 
Total construction of the wind farm components in Navajo County is expected to take less than one 
year, and the generation tie transmission line and switching station may be phased to be constructed 
prior to the components if this permit is approved.  The applicant has indicated in their submission that 
the construction phase of this projects is expected to create 200 plus construction jobs for its duration. 
 
ZONING DISTRICTS: 
ARTICLE 3 – (A-GENERAL) – GENERAL ZONING DISTRICT 
 
Section 301 – Purpose.  
  
The main purpose of this A-General Zone is to provide for all the unincorporated area of the County, 
except land within the boundary of reservation and outside the authority of Navajo County not 
otherwise designated for some other specific zone, to be incl uded in the “A -General Zone,” by this 
Ordinance.  No subdividing shall be conducted or approved in the “A -General Zone,” without prior 
re-zoning of the land so intended.  Uses permitted in the “A -General Zone,” include farm and non -
farm residential uses, farms, recreational, institutional, commercial and industrial uses as specifically 
listed in this Article.  Other uses may be permitted as Special Uses under Article 20.

<!-- page 570 -->
ARTICLE 8 – (RURAL 1) RURAL ZONING DISTRICT 
 ONE (1) ACRE PER DWELLING UNIT 
 
Section 801 – Purpose.  
 
The primary purpose of this district is to conserve and protect open land uses, foster orderly growth in 
rural areas, and prevent urban agricultural land use conflicts. The purpose of requiring large minimum 
parcels of not less than one (1) acre in area is to discourage small lot or residential subdivisions where 
public facilities such as water, sewage disposal, parks and playgrounds, and governmental services 
such as police and fire protection are not available or could not reasonably be made currently availab le.  
Uses permitted in this zoning district include both farm and non -farm residential uses, farms, and 
recreational and institutional uses. 
 
ZONING ORDINANCE: 
Article 20 – Special Uses and Planned Unit Developments 
 
Section 2001 – Special Uses  
  
The Board of Supervisors may permit as a Special Use the following uses in zoning districts 
from which they are otherwise prohibited by this Ordinance, unless any such use is further 
prohibited by this Article. 
 
 13. Electric power genera ting plants and facilities, including but not limited to those 
 operated by nuclear or fossil fuel or solar, wind or geothermal energy. 
 
COMPREHENSIVE PLAN/AREA PLAN:  
The subject properties are within the Rural Ranch character area of Navajo County.  The purpose of the 
Rural Ranch character area is to preserve the open character of land traditionally used for ranching in 
Navajo County.  Any industrial or storage uses in Rural Ranch should be screened from views from 
rights-of-way. 
 
4.0 Land Use Element 
 
4.7 Goals and Policies 
 
Goal 3:  To preserve and protect archaeological and historic resources for their aesthetic, 
scientific, educational, and cultural value. 
 
Policy 3-A: Where probable cause for discovery of cultural or archaeological resources exists, 
encourage property owner(s) to contact the Arizona State Historic Preservation Office. 
 
- The applicant has been working with consultants, SWCA, to conduct archival records 
reviews and pedestrian surveys for potentially distu rbed areas.  As of their submittal, they 
had found 14 historic and prehistoric sites within the Navajo County portion of the project.  
The intent is to report the findings of this survey to the ASLD and the Arizona State Historic 
Preservation Office.  If the project ends up needing to disturb ground outside where currently 
projected, there will be further pedestrian surveys.  On the State Trust Land, if areas are

<!-- page 571 -->
eligible for the Arizona Register of Historic Places (ARHP), they should be avoided.  If this 
is not possible, then they should be mitigated to prevent adverse effects.  On both private 
and State Trust Land, the applicant intends to avoid any sites recommended as register -
eligible, and if not possible, follow applicable laws. 
 
Goal 5: Improve the overall appearance of the County. 
  
 Policy 5-A: Maintain natural scenic qualities of the County by identifying and protecting cultural
 resources; protecting wildlife habitat; natural plant communities and riparian areas; and 
 encouraging protection of scenic vistas. 
 
- The development of this wind energy generation facility could have an impact on some of 
the scenic qualities of the County, though this would be expected with any project of this 
nature.  The applicant has made full efforts to identify cultural resources and will be using 
state guidelines to ensure protection of them to the greatest amount possible.  On the ground, 
this project has little to no effect on wildlife.  A Wildlife Site Evaluation was completed for 
all wildlife within project boundaries.  General concerns for this project are related to avian 
wildlife.  Through the help of a consulting firm and AGFD, the applicant has completed or 
is in the process of completing the following: Avian Use Counts – Large Bird Use Surveys, 
Avian Use Counts – Small Bird Surveys, Eagle and Other Raptor Species Nest Surveys, an 
Eagle Utilization Distribution Assessment, and Bat Acoustic Surveys .  The applicant has 
also met in person with and had consultation communications with the U.S. Fish and 
Wildlife Service.  Native Plant and Noxious Weed inventories were completed on the subject 
sites.  A Preliminary Jurisdictional Delineation for Water of the United States is also in the 
process of being completed by the applicant. 
 
Goal 6: Maintain compatible land use patterns while encouraging free market development.  
 
 Policy 6 -B: Consider, if neede d, providing buffers for different land uses including, but not 
 limited to, setbacks, walls or fences, and landscaping. 
 
- It is impossible to buffer objects like wind turbines through the use of walls, fences, and 
landscaping, as would be expected for smaller-scale projects.  Instead, the applicant will be 
following the setback requirements as laid out in Section 2008 for wind energy generatio n 
facilities.  The applicant has asked for a variance for setback requirements for three turbines 
(if the tallest turbine model is used) for properties that adjoin the Coconino County portion 
of the wind farm.  Coconino County has stated that they have no objection to the proposed 
tower locations shown on the site plan.  The Board of Supervisors may approve a reduction 
in the setback requirements laid out in Section 2008 if, “The project shares a common 
property line with another approved Wind Energy Generation facility.”  The applicant is 
asking for a variance where the project on the Navajo County side would be sharing  a 
common property line with the same project on the Coconino County side.  Ultimately, the 
Board of Supervisors will have to decide if they feel this variance request is appropriate 
given the circumstances.   
 
 Policy 6-C: Require paved or other appropriately surfaced access to commercial and industrial
 uses. 
 
- The majority of construction access for this project will come from the Coconino County 
side of State Route 99, an appropriately paved form of access to the project site.  For regular

<!-- page 572 -->
operation, the applicant has a primary choice of existing Forest Service Road coming from 
the Heber/Overgaard area and a secondary choice of Hutch Road.  With the projected 
staffing levels post-construction, and the limited amount of this project being within Navajo 
County’s jurisdiction, the abovementioned roads should serve adequate for the project.  
 
Goal 7: Facilitate commercial and industrial development, including business and technology 
uses, where appropriate, to increase the sales tax and employment opportunities. 
 
 Policy 7 -B: Encourage the development of non -resource specific industrial uses along major 
 roadways, rail heads, and airports and the development of resource specific industrial uses in 
 appropriate remote locations. 
  
- The development of a wind energy generation facility is resource specific in nature.  As such, 
the fairly remote location of Chevelon Canyon, off State Route 99 appears to be appropriate 
for developments like a wind energy generation facility.  This mitigates their general impact 
on the public health, safety, and welfare. 
 
5.0 Circulation Element  
 
5.4 Goals and Policies 
 
Goal 1: Provide a range of circulation options that are safe and efficient and that complement 
local communities and the natural environment. 
 
 Policy 1 -B: Coordinate land use and circulation planning to encourage comprehensive and
 efficient development and growth patterns that support adjacent land uses, complement the
 character of adjacent communities and neighborhoods, and mitigate impac ts on the natural
 environment. 
 
- Properties in the vicinity are generally vacant, grazing land, or single family residential.  
With this in mind, a wind farm would not necessarily support or complement these uses.  
Wind farms do, however, require large amou nts of land, typically further away from high 
density population centers.  In this regard, this region is suitable for developments of this 
nature.  Additionally, the applicant is completing a number of studies and will have 
requirements to fulfill with their project that mitigate impacts to the natural environment. 
 
Analysis: 
 
Typical development standard concerns do not apply to a project of this scale that spans nearly 6 
different sections of land on its Navajo County side.  With such a large amount of land being involved, 
there are not concerns over typical yard setbacks, lot area, lot coverage, lot width, or distance between 
structures as all of these requirements are far exceeded within the project boundary. 
 
This project has met, or is in the process of meeting, a number of goals laid out in the Navajo County 
Comprehensive Plan.  The applicant had a consulting firm complete archival reviews and pedestrian 
surveys to identify cultural and historic resources.  With these findings, the applicant has created plans 
that are in line with state regulations to deal with potential cultural and historic resources on site. 
 
As far as protecting wildlife habitat and natural plant communities, the applicant has met or exceeded 
requirements of Navajo County and other government agencies involved with the project.  They have

<!-- page 573 -->
completed, or are in the process of completing, a Wildlife Site Evaluation, Avian Use Counts – Large 
Bird Use Surveys, Avian Use Counts – Small Bird Surveys, Eagle and Other Raptor Species Nest 
Surveys, an Eagle Utilization Distribution Assessment, and Bat Acoustic Surveys.  As far as plants, 
there have been N ative Plant and Noxious Weed inventories completed on the subject sites.   A 
Preliminary Jurisdictional Delineation for Water of the United States is also in the process of completio n 
by the applicant. 
 
There is appropriate access to this site, via State Route 99, which is planned to be utilized during the 
construction phase and runs through this project on both the Coconino and Navajo County sides.  Once 
construction is complete, less developed roads will be used, though staffing levels will have de creased 
significantly, leaving little cause for concern. 
 
The only component of the Navajo County Comprehensive Plan that cannot be addressed is the project’s 
potential impact to scenic vistas.  Due to the height of the proposed turbines, there will be an unavoidab le 
impact on the skyline in Navajo County, which can hardly be mitigated by increased setbacks from 
other properties. 
 
The applicant held two public outreach meetings, one within Coconino County and one within Navajo 
County as the proposed project crosses the jurisdictional boundaries.  The applicant hosted their public 
outreach meeting in Navajo County  for both Navajo and Coconino Count ies on July 15 th, 2019 in 
Winslow.  Notification of this meeting was posted in the July 3 rd edition of The Holbrook Tribune and 
July 2nd edition of the Arizona Daily Sun. Notification letters were also mailed to applicants within a 2-
mile radius of the proposed project on July 1st.  
 
In addition to the meetings and mailings, the applicant created a website for their project, 
chevelonbuttewind.spower.com, which allows people to inform themselves on the plans for the project, 
look at visual simulations, and provide comments of concern or support for the project. 
 
Comments from the public were solicited through the various forms of outreach completed by the 
applicant.  The most common concerns raised over the project were visibility, affected property values, 
location in relation to properties, access,  noise impact, impact to cultural and historic resources,  the 
ability to distribute electricity in the area,  financial guarantees for decommissioning, and fire risk. 
 
At the Planning and Zoning Commission meeting held on October 17 th, 2019, a recommendation was 
made to the Navajo County Board of Supervisors to approve th e Special Use Permit subject to the 
conditions included in this report and the condition that items 5.i and 13 of the conditions be revised by 
staff, the applicant, and counsel by a vote of 3 -2.  Staff, counsel, and the applicant have come to an 
agreement regarding the revision of these conditions. 
 
FINDINGS OF FACT: 
 
1. The item has been properly noticed and posted in compliance with Arizona Revised Statutes 
and Article 29.  
 
Postcards were sent out for this item on Tuesday, November 5 th, 2019.  The property itself was 
posted on Thursday, November 21st, 2019.  A legal ad notice was posted in The Holbrook Tribune 
on Wednesday, November 20th, 2019. 
 
2. The proposal is in compliance with the Comprehensive Plan.

<!-- page 574 -->
This project and the work done to mitigate impacts fit almost completely with goals, policies, and 
actions of the Comprehensive Plan.  The only area where there is a potential issue and conflict with 
the Comprehensive Plan is protecting the County’s scenic vistas. 
 
3. The proposed use  is compatible with the permissible uses in the zoning district in which the 
property is located. 
 
The proposed use is not allowed by -right in the zoning district in which the property is located, 
which is why a Special Use Permit is being requested. 
 
4. The proposed use is  compatible with the current and likely future uses of properties in the 
vicinity of the proposed use.  
 
For the most part, land in the area is either vacant, single-family residential, or grazing land.  This 
proposed use should not have adverse effects on these uses in the area, especially given the large 
setbacks for the turbines from the project boundary and existing residences. 
 
5. The proposed use will have minimal adverse effects on the public health, safety, and general 
welfare of properties in the vicinity of the proposed use. 
 
The addition of wind turbines to the subject properties should not have adverse effects on public 
health, safety, or general welfare in the vicinity of the proposed use.
